strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP evaluation problem. Distinguishing subject overlap, repeated stimulus text, and overlapping fMRI windows identifies concrete risks when measuring generalization to unseen subjects and language.

Experiments cover two modalities, two established decoding frameworks, and several splitting strategies. The additional-test and shuffled-input diagnostics expose substantial sensitivity of reported performance to evaluation conditions.

Table 6 provides useful free-generation results: differences between splitting strategies persist without teacher forcing. This offers preliminary evidence that the concern extends beyond reference-prefix access alone.
weaknesses: The published algorithms do not enforce the central zero-leakage guarantee. Algorithm 1, line 15, checks subject membership when expanding training edges but permits held-out texts to enter training. Algorithm 2, line 33, checks story membership but permits held-out subjects to enter training. Both endpoints must satisfy the partition constraints in Equations 13–14. Consequently, the pseudocode can recreate the very overlap the method claims to eliminate.

The main benchmark uses teacher forcing during evaluation: Table 5 reproduces the teacher-forced values in Table 6. These scores measure predictions conditioned on reference prefixes, limiting their interpretation as autonomous brain-to-text generation. For example, ZuCo UniCoRN BLEU-1 falls from 23.32 to 14.02 without teacher forcing. The appendix partially addresses this issue, but does not repeat the additional-test and shuffled-input diagnostics under free generation.

The leakage metrics are not consistently specified. Equation 17 counts exact signal intersection, whereas the stated definition concerns shared subject identity. Disjoint EEG examples from the same subject would have zero signal intersection despite satisfying the paper's subject-overlap criterion, leaving Table 2's nonzero rates unexplained. Subjects absent from training also create an unspecified zero denominator. Equations 6–7 incorrectly require every training example to have a matching test subject or stimulus, although a single overlapping pair should suffice.

The experiments do not adequately isolate the claimed mechanisms. Splitting strategies change training-data quantity and subject/story distributions alongside overlap. Decreasing reconstruction loss on a validation set containing familiar subjects does not establish that representations are degrading, and continued test-score improvement is not a general diagnostic of leakage. Matched training sizes and evaluation on a common clean holdout are needed to substantiate these causal claims.

Reproducibility is insufficient for a proposed benchmark. The manuscript does not link executable code or concrete split manifests, report retained/discarded sample counts, identify the final subject/story partitions after filtering, or adequately specify the additional test set and shuffling procedure. Four seeds are reported for leakage rates, but decoding results lack variability across training runs or held-out groups. These omissions are consequential given the algorithmic inconsistencies.

Numerical reporting requires an audit. Table 5 reports EEG2Text ROUGE-1 F=25.74 with precision=23.95 and recall=23.98, incompatible with standard, consistently aggregated F1. The Narratives method-(a) value 40.65 is labeled F in Table 3 but recall in Table 7. Appendix E also describes EEG method (d) as lacking text leakage, contradicting the main analysis and Table 2. These discrepancies weaken confidence in the benchmark and comparisons.

The universal framing exceeds the supported contribution. Joint subject-and-stimulus holdout is appropriate for simultaneous generalization along both axes; other splits can legitimately evaluate narrower targets. Examining two models does not establish that all previous evaluations are meaningless. Appendix D's claim that discarding samples is always necessary also lacks a connectivity assumption: disconnected subject-stimulus components can be partitioned without discarding data. The useful evaluation concern merits further work, but the implementation, measurement, and experimental issues require revision before a sound, reproducible Findings recommendation.
